name: Upland Vernacular Greek Revival

revival_periods.note: The contemporary market's 'modern farmhouse' takes its silhouette from exactly this stratum - plain gable, wide flat trim, no ornament - while omitting the proportional rules that made the plainness legible.

geography.hearth: East Tennessee and the Kentucky Bluegrass

lineage.note: The center-passage plan, the gable-end chimneys and the tall single-pile section arrive from here; the Grecian trim is a change of profile on an unchanged house.

Extremely common and routinely missed: an existing log house is weatherboarded, given a Grecian doorway, corner pilasters and a frieze board, and thereafter reads as a frame Greek Revival house. Many 'Greek Revival' I-houses in the uplands have logs inside their walls.

description.short: The Greek Revival reduced to its cheapest legible signals - a heavy doorway, wide corner boards, a frieze under the eave - applied to the ordinary two-storey single-pile farmhouse of the Upland South and the Ohio Valley, frequently over a log core.
description.long:
This is the Greek Revival as most Americans actually encountered it, and it is almost entirely a matter of trim. The house underneath is the one the region was already building: two storeys tall, one room deep, a central passage running front to back, chimneys at both gable ends, a porch across the front. What the Grecian moment adds is a set of boards. The corner boards widen from four inches to ten or twelve and acquire a cap, so they read as pilasters. A frieze board a foot deep runs under the eave, and the cornice returns are clipped across the gable base. The door surround becomes a rectangular transom with sidelights inside broad flat pilasters carrying a heavy flat entablature - copied, usually badly and always confidently, from a plate in Benjamin or Lafever that a local carpenter owned or had seen. Nothing else changes. The plan does not change, the framing does not change, the chimneys do not move. This is the mechanism by which a national style becomes a vernacular one: it arrives as a set of profiles that can be run with planes a carpenter already owns, and it costs the price of wider boards.

The conditions are those of a cash-poor but land-rich agricultural society reaching a modest surplus at exactly the moment the style was available. The Upland South and the Ohio Valley filled with Scots-Irish, German and Virginia migrant families between 1780 and 1830; by the 1840s the successful among them were replacing log houses with frame or brick ones, or - just as often - encasing the log house they already had. Water-powered sawmills on every creek supplied the wide boards; itinerant carpenters carried the handbooks; and the whole transformation could be accomplished a piece at a time. The result is a landscape where the same house form runs from a two-room log pen to a full brick I-house with a Grecian doorway, and the Greek Revival content of any given example is a fair measure of how good the last twenty years had been.

What it reacts against is not Federal - most of these builders never built a Federal house - but plainness itself, and the reaction is careful and cheap. There is no portico on the ordinary example, because a portico costs columns; there is a shed or hip porch on square or chamfered posts, and where a builder could afford it those posts get a bevel and a cap that gesture at an order. The most interesting quality of the stratum is its discipline: because there is no ornament to hide behind, the proportions have to carry the building, and the good ones are good almost entirely because the frieze depth, the trim widths and the roof pitch are right. The bad ones fail for exactly the same reason, which is the argument for encoding the ratios rather than the mouldings.

Standing in front of one, on a ridge road in East Tennessee or on a Bluegrass turnpike, the first impression is of a very tall, very thin house. The I-house is two storeys and one room deep, so from the gable end it is a slab, and the eave assembly is the only heavy thing on it. The doorway is where all the money went and it is out of scale in a way that is entirely satisfying: a fifteen-hundred-square-foot farmhouse with an entrance surround that would look correct on a courthouse. Inside, the passage runs straight through with a door at each end, the stair goes up one wall, the rooms are twelve feet square with plain heavy architraves and a mantel of two flat pilasters and a shelf, and everything is painted or whitewashed. In August, with both passage doors open, the house works exactly as the dogtrot works, which is the point: the same climate logic runs from the log pens through this stratum and up into the plantation houses, and only the amount of trim changes.

defining_characteristics: Greek Revival present as trim profile only: wide corner pilaster boards, deep plain frieze, clipped cornice returns, heavy flat door surround
Underlying plan unchanged from regional practice - two-storey single-pile with central passage, or double-pen, or hall-and-parlor
Rectangular-transom entrance with sidelights in a broad pilastered surround, disproportionately grand relative to the house
Gable-end chimneys, frequently exterior, retained from the region's earlier practice
Front porch on plain square or chamfered posts rather than a classical portico
Roof pitch dropped to 5:12-7:12 from the steeper pitches of the log and Federal-era work it replaces
Frequent log or hewn-timber core concealed inside a weatherboarded frame wall
diagnostic_tells: A courthouse-scale doorway on a farmhouse-scale building - the surest sign of the stratum
Corner boards 10-12 inches wide with a simple capital, and no columns anywhere on the building
Two-storey, one-room-deep silhouette (I-house) with a heavy eave band - it is a facade from the road and a wall from the side
Porch posts chamfered with a lamb's-tongue stop instead of turned or classical columns
Weatherboard that steps oddly around a thicker wall zone, or window jambs unusually deep: there are logs inside

distinguished_from.difference: A matter of two orders of magnitude in cost and of the presence or absence of an actual order. The plantation variant has a colossal colonnade, 12-14 foot ceilings and a detached kitchen; this stratum has trim boards, 9-10 foot ceilings, a rear kitchen ell and no columns.

The Northern variant turns the gable to the road and builds compactly with a side-hall plan; the Upland variant keeps the broadside I-house with a central passage open at both ends, because it is solving for summer heat rather than for winter.

Direct descendant and often indistinguishable on a bad day. The Greek Revival stratum keeps the classical trim discipline - continuous frieze, pilastered corners, entablature over the door. Once the frieze becomes a plain fascia and the doorway loses its entablature, the building has crossed into the un-styled farmhouse.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Classical proportion carried entirely by board width and eave depth, with no orders present. The frieze-to-storey-height and trim-width ratios are what make the building legible as classical; when they are wrong the house simply looks like a plain box, which is exactly what happened after 1875.
typical_ratios: Frieze board 10-16 inches on a two-storey house; total eave assembly 14-22 inches
Corner pilaster boards 10-12 inches wide, projecting 1-1.5 inches, with a 2-3 inch cap
Door surround: pilasters 6-9 inches wide, entablature 12-18 inches deep, opening 4.5-6 feet wide overall with sidelights
I-house depth 16-20 feet single-pile; passage 8-12 feet wide
Roof pitch 5:12 to 7:12; cornice returns 10-18 inches
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Three or five even bays broadside to the road with the door centred on the passage; the rhythm is the plan's, not the style's, and the trim simply marks it.

massing_affinities.note: Two storeys, one room deep, three to five bays - the definitive Upland South statement of arrival, and the substrate this variant dresses.
Where Northern settlement reached the Ohio Valley the upright-and-wing appears with the same Grecian trim.
The two-door, two-room house with Grecian corner boards - the cheapest possible expression of the stratum.
Dogtrots were routinely weatherboarded and given Grecian doorways at both ends of the passage in the 1840s-50s.

constraints.statement: A continuous frieze board of at least 10 inches (14-16 on a two-storey house) must run under the eave on all elevations, with corner pilaster boards no less than 10 inches wide. Below these widths the classical reading collapses and the building is simply a plain farmhouse.

test.note: Tests the frieze/eave trim board width floor (10in minimum; 14-16in on a two-storey house is a further refinement left as prose). Corner pilaster board width (also 10in minimum) has no separate vocabulary variable and stays prose too.

constraints.statement: Entrance must be a rectangular opening with a rectangular transom, sidelights optional, inside flat pilasters carrying a flat entablature at least 12 inches deep. Elliptical fanlights, arched openings and applied Adamesque ornament are forbidden.

Where a central passage is used it must be operable at both ends and the main block must remain single-pile (16-20 feet deep). Doubling the depth without adding cross-ventilation converts a working summer plan into a dark box.

test.note: Tests the single-pile depth range (16-20ft). The passage-operable-at-both-ends clause is left as prose -- no vocabulary variable expresses passage door operability.

constraints.statement: Free-standing classical columns are out of character; porch supports are square or chamfered posts 4x4 to 6x6, chamfer stopped 12-18 inches from deck and soffit. If columns are wanted, the building belongs to a different variant.

Where a log core is encased, the weatherboard must be furred out to a consistent plane and window jambs detailed for a wall 8-12 inches thick; the deep reveal is a legitimate and legible feature, not a defect to be concealed.

test.note: Tests the wall-thickness range where a log core is encased. The furring-consistency requirement is left as prose.

exemplars.name: DeVault-Massengill House
exemplars.note: Built by Isaac DeVault; upland East Tennessee Greek Revival on a farm whose earlier circa-1769 log house survives on the same property - the whole log-to-Grecian sequence in one place.

exemplars.name: Swaim House
exemplars.note: Circa 1840s; a plain Greek Revival farmhouse in the Middle Tennessee uplands, listed on the National Register in 1984. Ordinary in the way this stratum is ordinary, which is why it is worth recording.

sources: Henry Glassie, Folk Housing in Middle Virginia (1975)
Talbot Hamlin, Greek Revival Architecture in America (1944)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2013)
Asher Benjamin, The Architect, or Practical House Carpenter (1830)
Tennessee Historical Commission National Register nomination files

proportion_packs.note: Bind the wall_section_greek_revival / casing_greek_revival family for the 'plain heavy architraves and a mantel of two flat pilasters and a shelf' the style's own description gives its interiors. NO ORDER PACK IS BOUND ON THIS NODE, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight -- see the report. This entry only covers the interior wall trim; the exterior frieze-board and corner-pilaster system that is this style's actual proportional identity (governing_logic: 'classical proportion carried entirely by board width and eave depth, with no orders present') has no dedicated pack anywhere in the 36. That is a genuine, acknowledged gap, not something this binding claims to solve.

Governs the doorway the style calls 'a courthouse-scale doorway on a farmhouse-scale building -- the surest sign of the stratum' and its own diagnostic tell. Constraint c02 (rectangular transom, sidelights optional, entablature at least 12 in deep, no ellipses or arches) is the style's hard rule layered on top of this pack's general door-sizing logic.
The window-glazing module. Bound but genuinely secondary here -- this style's own diagnostic_tells are all about board width and doorway scale, and sash pattern is not named among them at all.

The one Greek Revival node in this batch that gets room-vernacular rather than room-harmonic, and the corpus's own applies_to cross-reference lists it here specifically -- correctly, since the style's own governing_logic states the underlying plan (I-house, double-pen, dogtrot) is unchanged regional practice that predates the Grecian trim moment entirely: '12 feet square with plain heavy architraves,' composed by inherited habit rather than by a pattern-book room-generating ratio.

Bound for the frequent and 'routinely missed' log core this style hybridizes with -- an existing log pen weatherboarded and given Grecian trim, per the style's own lineage note and constraint c05 (encased log core, wall 8-12 in thick, furred to a consistent plane). The corpus's own applies_to cross-reference lists this node for log-module directly.

The frame (non-log) construction mode -- the weatherboarded I-house or double-pen built new in frame rather than encasing an existing log pen. Bound optional and below log-module because the style's own long description treats the log-to-frame sequence as the more distinctive and more often overlooked case.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's own notes state its subject as Vignola's Ionic order in full -- module of 18 parts, column 18 modules, pedestal 6, base, shaft, capital, volute and fluting -- every one of those figures measured off the semidiameter of a column at the base of the shaft. The node's governing_logic states in words that its classical reading is carried by board width and eave depth with no orders present, and its own tell records 'no columns anywhere on the building', so the datum this pack measures from does not exist on this building. This is not the blanket-refusal trap: the node HAS a proportional system and states it precisely, in trim widths and eave depths, and what it refuses is specifically an order. Its distinguished_from entry for the plantation variant turns on 'the presence or absence of an actual order' and puts this stratum on the absent side.
declined_packs.quote: Classical proportion carried entirely by board width and eave depth, with no orders present.
declined_packs.note: governs 0 slots; 0 lose all dimensioning; declining changes no dimension on this node -- trim-classical, bound directly at precedence 1, already wins every trim slot (baseboard, casing, chair_rail, wainscot, door_surround, window_surround_wood) this order pack could otherwise have reached. No node descends from greek-revival-upland-vernacular, so the decline does not propagate.

declined_packs.reason: The pack's notes are explicit that it is about the colonnade and not the order -- 'how many columns there are, where they stand, what they stand on, or what the wall behind them is doing' -- and the one slot it governs here, composition_parti, it dimensions with portico_share, corner_contraction and centre_bay_widening, all three of which presuppose a portico of columns on the front. The node's description refuses the portico by name and gives the reason, and continues that the support is 'a shed or hip porch on square or chamfered posts'; constraint c04 adds that free-standing classical columns are out of character. The pack's portico_share rule asks what fraction of the front the portico takes on an elevation that has no portico, and its corner_contraction rule asks about a Doric frieze over column axes on a building whose frieze is a board. The record contradicts the pack's stated subject rather than merely being silent about it.
declined_packs.quote: There is no portico on the ordinary example, because a portico costs columns
declined_packs.note: governs 1 slot, composition_parti; 0 slots lose all dimensioning; on decline composition_parti passes to facade-medieval-english (jacobean). Recorded honestly: that fallback is not obviously right for an upland I-house either -- a decline stops a wrong pack and does not supply a right one, and the node's own trim-classical binding note already names the missing exterior frieze-board and corner-pilaster pack as 'a genuine, acknowledged gap'. No node descends from greek-revival-upland-vernacular, so the decline does not propagate.
